text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Peacock v. Tourism British Columbia,

2010 BCSC 93

Date: 20100125

Docket:
43435

Registry: Kamloops

Between:

Tammy
Peacock dba The Rock & River Rustic Retreat

Plaintiff

And

Tourism
British Columbia, Wanda Hook, Brent Hegadorn,

Julian Malinsky, Peter Walters, Sherry Eland, Anton Forester,

Rob Giffone, Piere Drouxin, Rod Harris,

Her Majesty the Queen in Right of the Province of British Columbia

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Hyslop

Reasons for Judgment

Tammy
Peacock appeared on her own behalf:

Counsel for Tourism British Columbia:

K. Horsman

Place and Date of Hearing:

Kamloops, B.C.

December 8, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

Kamloops, B.C.

January 25, 2010

[
1
]

The defendants seek to strike out the
plaintiff’s, Tammy Peacock, statement of claim in its entirety.  The defendants
rely on Rule 19(24) of the
Rules of Court
(the “
Rules
”).

[
2
]

On the date that I heard this application, I
struck out the entire statement of claim filed by Ms. Peacock, with costs in
the cause.  I also ordered that, if Ms. Peacock wished to pursue this action,
she file a new statement of claim within 60 days of the hearing of this
application.  In addition, I ordered that all pre-trial discovery processes be
stayed until the statement of claim is re-filed.  After making these orders I
agreed to give written reasons.  These are my reasons.

BACKGROUND

[
3
]

Ms. Peacock operates a tourist facility called
the Rock & River Rustic Retreat (the “facility”) on the South Thompson
River, near Walhachin, British Columbia.

[
4
]

In 2000, Ms. Peacock was approved by the
defendant, Tourism British Columbia, and the Ministry of Transportation and
Highways (Kamloops Division) (“MOTH”) as eligible for a blue and white highway
sign.  This sign gives the travelling public information on the location and
amenities of the facility.  The program required the payment of a fee and
periodic inspections of the facility.  In the summer of 2008, the facility
failed its inspection.  A controversy arose and the sign was removed in
September of 2008.

[
5
]

In the summer of 2009, the facility passed its
inspection and the blue and white sign was replaced.

[
6
]

Ms. Peacock argues that the facility, as a
result of the actions of the defendants, was adversely affected economically by
its interruption in the 2008 season and permanently impaired in the 2009
season.

[
7
]

Ms. Peacock brought her complaints to government
and to the Ombudsman.  On October 26, 2009, this action was commenced by Ms.
Peacock by filing a writ and statement of claim.

[
8
]

Tourism British Columbia is a Crown corporation.

[
9
]

The defendant, Wanda Hook, is employed by
Tourism British Columbia as a product service manager.

[
10
]

Brent Hegadorn is employed by Tourism British
Columbia as a coordinator for quality assurance.

[
11
]

The defendants, Julian Malinsky and Sherry
Eland, are managers for the MOTH.

[
12
]

Peter Walters is an assistant deputy to the
Minister of British Columbia responsible for Tourism, Culture and the Arts.

[
13
]

Anton Foreseter is an independent contractor
hired by Tourism British Columbia to inspect facilities.

[
14
]

Piere Drouxin is a manager of quality assurance
for Tourism British Columbia in the Vancouver office.  Though named in the
style of cause, he is not described in the statement of claim.

[
15
]

Rod Harris is the former chief executive officer
of Tourism British Columbia.

[
16
]

Bill Bennett is a former Minister of Tourism,
Culture and the Arts.

[
17
]

Robert MacKay-Dunn is Mr. Bennett’s
administrative assistant.

[
18
]

Neither Messrs. Bennett nor MacKay-Dunn appear
in the writ’s style of cause.  At the hearing of this application, I told Ms.
Peacock that if she wished to pursue claims against them, she would be required
to make an application to court to add them as defendants.

POSITIONS

[
19
]

The defendants allege that the statement of
claim, as drafted, does not disclose a reasonable cause of action against the
defendants.  The defendants allege that the statement of claim is prolix,
confusing, and does not permit the defendants to know the case against them and
should be struck out.  The defendants focus on Rule 19(24)(a), (b) and (c) of the

Rules
.

[
20
]

Ms. Peacock’s position is that she has been
wronged, she is unrepresented and the statement of claim she filed is the best
she can do.  In her response to Karen Horsman’s outline, Ms. Peacock writes:

My claim is
simple - - I have experienced significant loss due to the unlawful, high-handed
and negligent actions of government officials, and I am seeking compensation
for it.

THE LAW

[
21
]

The purpose of pleadings, in this case the
statement of claim, is to clearly define the issues of fact and law to be determined
by the court.  In
Homalco Indian Band v. British Columbia
,
1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
, [1998] B.C.J.
No. 2703, Mr. Justice K. Smith summarizes the law as follows:

[6]        A useful description of the
proper structure of a plea of a cause of action is set out in J.H. Koffler and A.
Reppy, Handbook of Common Law Pleading, (St. Paul, Minn.: West Publishing Co.,
1969) at p. 85:

Of course the
essential elements of any claim of relief or remedial right will vary from
action to action. But, on analysis, the pleader will find that the facts
prescribed by the substantive law as necessary to constitute a cause of action
in a given case, may be classified under three heads: (1) The plaintiff's right
or title; (2) The defendant's wrongful act violating that right or title; (3)
The consequent damage, whether nominal or substantial. And, of course, the
facts constituting the cause of action should be stated with certainty and
precision, and in their natural order, so as to disclose the three elements
essential to every cause of action, to wit, the right, the wrongful act and the
damage.

If the
statement of claim is to serve the ultimate purpose of pleadings, the material
facts of each cause of action relied upon should be set out in the above
manner. As well, they should be stated succinctly and the particulars should
follow and should be identified as such: Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers
Inc. (1988),
1988 CanLII 2832 (BC CA)
, 26 B.C.L.R. (2d) 349 (C.A.) at 353.

[
22
]

The requirements of pleadings are stated in Rule
19 of the
Rules
:

Rule 19 — Pleadings Generally

Contents

(1)  A pleading shall be as brief as
the nature of the case will permit and must contain a statement in summary form
of the material facts on which the party relies, but not the evidence by which
the facts are to be proved.

…

Form

(5)  A pleading shall be divided into paragraphs
numbered consecutively, each allegation being contained in a separate
paragraph.

…

Scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious matters

(24)  At any stage of a proceeding the court may order
to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement, pleading,
petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses no
reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b) it is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may prejudice,
embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d) it is otherwise an abuse
of the process of the court,

and the court may grant judgment
or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of
the application to be paid as special costs.

[
23
]

Assuming the facts as stated in the statement of
claim can be proved, the question then becomes: Is it “plain and obvious” that
Ms. Peacock’s statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action?” (
Budgell
v. Oppal,
2007 BCSC 991
).

[
24
]

A statement of claim should not be struck if
there is a chance Ms. Peacock may succeed.  The novelty of the claim, nor the
strength of the defendants’ case, should prevent Ms. Peacock from proceeding.

Only if the
action is certain to fail because it contains a radical defect ranking with the
others listed in Rule 19(24)

of the British
Columbia
Rules of Court
should the relevant portions of a
plaintiff's statement of claim be struck out under Rule 19(24)(a). [
Budgell
,
para.
7]

[
25
]

Rule 19(1) of the
Rules
requires the
pleadings be brief and must contain material facts in summary form on which Ms.
Peacock relies.  If the material fact is not plead, then the pleadings will not
withstand the application of the defendants.  Madam Justice Ross in
Budgell

said:

[9]        The
issue is not whether the plaintiff has failed to identify the specific causes
of action or tort claims advanced. Rather, the Court is to examine the
statement of claim to see whether the material facts set out would, if proved,
complete all the constitutent elements of causes of action known in law: see
Alford v. Canada (Attorney General) (1997),
1997 CanLII 868 (BC SC)
, 31 B.C.L.R. (3d) 228 (S.C.) per
Brenner J. at 235 and 236.

ANALYSIS

[
26
]

Keeping these principles in mind, I will examine
the statement of claim filed by Ms. Peacock.

[
27
]

After describing some of the defendants in the
statement of claim, Ms. Peacock presents this heading in her statement of claim
“
Misfeasance in public office
”.  Following this heading, paragraphs 12
to 30 appear.  The next heading is “
Relief Requested
”, and the following
is sought under that heading:

[WHEREFORE] the Plaintiff claims against the
Defendants jointly and severly:

The Plaintiff’s claim is for a declaration
and damages for injury suffered due to misfeasance in public office or
negligence in the performance of a public duty, or acting without authority,
plus punitive or exemplary damages and costs.  Such further or other relief as to
this Honourable Court seems just.

A letter of apology from the ministry.

A Declaration
that the Plaintiff may apply for, and receive highway signs for the business
independent of TCA.

[
28
]

In
Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3
S.C.R. 263, Mr. Justice Iacobucci defined the tort of misfeasance in public
office as:

[32]      To
summarize, I am of the opinion that the tort of misfeasance in a public office
is an intentional tort whose distinguishing elements are twofold: (i)
deliberate unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions; and (ii)
awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff.
Alongside deliberate unlawful conduct and the requisite knowledge, a plaintiff
must also prove the other requirements common to all torts. More specifically,
[page287] the plaintiff must prove that the tortious conduct was the legal
cause of his or her injuries, and that the injuries suffered are compensable in
tort law.

[
29
]

In paragraph 12 of the statement of claim, Ms.
Peacock appears to attempt to allege misfeasance in public office by Wanda
Hook, who Ms. Peacock alleges conspired with others to “maliciously discredit”
the facility.  The allegation does not state what Ms. Hook did, with whom she
conspired and what it is she did to discredit the facility.

[
30
]

Similarly, in paragraph 17 of the statement of
claim, it is alleged that the defendants used not only excessive power (power
they were not authorized to use by public servants), used it maliciously and
with intent to harm the facility with the knowledge of reckless indifference
that the facility would suffer substantial losses.  As in paragraph 12, this
paragraph lacks material facts to support a claim for misfeasance in public
office.  The defendant or the defendants, who are alleged to have exceeded their
authority are not named or identified, the acts for which they exceed their
authority are not identified, and when the deliberate act or acts complained of
occurred.

[
31
]

Paragraph 13 is descriptive.

[
32
]

Paragraph 14 sets out no cause of action, is
descriptive, as well as being critical of government policy as it relates to
highway signage generally.

[
33
]

Paragraph 15 alleges that the defendant, Wanda
Hook, and others, labelled the facility as substandard and not meeting certain
standards, (by implication as not being true) and “other untruthful slanderous
labels and accusations.”  This attempt to allege defamation is not made out.
The material facts are not plead.  They do not consist of the words “spoken”
that are alleged to have been slanderous, to whom the words were spoken, who
spoke the words and when the words were spoken.

[
34
]

Paragraph 16 of the statement of claim alleges
that the defendants communicated:

... slanderous
un-truths and accusations, discrediting the plaintiff’s business and reputation
in the public eye and amongst key decision makers within the ministry of
transportation and highways.

This allegation suffers from the shortfalls
to which I refer to in paragraph 15 of the statement of claim.

[
35
]

Paragraph 18 and the two numbered paragraphs 19,
do not refer to any tort or cause of action.  None of the defendants are
identified and they are lumped together with no allegation as to what it is
that they did.  There is no tort known for failure to provide dispute
resolution.

[
36
]

Paragraph 21 of the statement of claim alleges
that the defendant, Peter Walters, failed to help the plaintiff.  There is
nothing in that paragraph that pleads a cause of action against Mr. Walters or
anyone else.

[
37
]

Paragraphs 22 and 23 seem to relate to a
judicial review that Ms. Peacock started.  Although the subject matter of the
judicial review is the subject matter of this action, it is not relevant to
this litigation and does not disclose or assist in the disclosure of a cause of
action.

[
38
]

Ms. Peacock, in paragraph 24, describes the
events that led to her obtaining approval of the facility, making it eligible
for blue and white highway signs again.  In that paragraph, she states that she
disapproved of the inspectors chosen to inspect the facility, and the money she
spent for the approval.  Ms. Peacock complains in paragraph 25, that Ms. Hook
and Mr. Hegadorn prevented her from advertising a cabin at the facility and
accuses them of making errors and omissions concerning the facility in the
printed guide produced by Tourism British Columbia.  These allegations offend
Rule 19(24)(b) and (c) of the
Rules
in that they are unnecessary and
vexatious (
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160).

[
39
]

Paragraphs 27, 28, 29 and 30 are statements
which have little to do with the issues that Ms. Peacock is trying to raise;
they are embarrassing and scandalous.

[
40
]

Under the relief requested, Ms. Peacock seeks
damages, among other matters, for “injury due to ... or negligence in the
performance of a public duty”.  The statement of claim does not assert that one
or more of the defendants owe the plaintiff a duty of care, the basis of that
duty of care, and the actions of defendants failing to meet the standard of
care.  Ms. Peacock has not plead the material facts to support a claim in
negligence against any of the defendants.

[
41
]

It is for these reasons that Ms. Peacock’s
statement of claim was struck out with costs in the cause.

“H.C. Hyslop J.”

HYSLOP J.
